To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

rare coding variants in HNF1α that result in reduced HNF-α transcriptional activity are strongly associated with diabetes, but rare coding variants that are predicted by bioinformatics tools as likely pathogenic are not associated with diabetes.
functional investigations of HNF1α variants identified in the general population can inform models of type 2 diabetes risk prediction.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the genetic basis of type 2 diabetes and the identification of genetic markers that can inform risk prediction models for this common disease.
the genetic architecture of type 2 diabetes (T2D) and its related phenotypes.
the identification of genetic variants that predispose to type 2 diabetes in the general (non-MODY) population and their use for the purposes of risk prediction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the variants in the MODY3 gene HNF1A are associated with a risk of developing type 2 diabetes, and that these variants are more frequent in people with diabetes than in the general population
the HNF1A gene harbours rare variants that are associated with diabetes in a dose-dependent fashion, with the strongest effects seen for those variants that are most likely to be pathogenic.
the HNF1A variant rs1170802 (Gly115Asp) is associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, whereas the HNF1α Gly115Ala variant (rs1169288) is not.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the HNF1A gene is associated with a rare, but important, risk for type 2 diabetes in the general European population.
the functional investigation of variants in MODY genes can be used to predict diabetes in the general populations.
functional characterization of HNF1a variants can identify a subset of variants that confer risk for type 2 diabetes in the general populations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
functional classification of Hnf1a variants can inform models that predict risk of type 2 diabetes in the general populations.
rare variants in HNF1α are associated with diabetes in a general population, but that the association depends on the functional impact of the variants.
